tickets.title: Deploy delta: scan sandbox image, tool/rulepack db-sync job, scratch tmpfs + runbook
acceptance: Scan sandbox image (semgrep/syft/grype at pinned versions with checksums) builds in CI; quadlet/compose units run scan workers with the docs/design/SECURITY_SUITE.md §2.2 profile — non-root, --network=none, ro,noexec snapshot mount, pids/CPU/mem caps, no secrets mounted (NFR-14, SC-27/SC-28)

Nightly host-side db-sync job refreshes grype/OSV/KEV data + custom semgrep pack volumes from pinned, checksum-verified sources into read-only volumes; scan containers themselves never get network; SCAN_SCRATCH_ROOT tmpfs sizing + sweeper documented in docs/RUNBOOK.md
Prod smoke: manual 'scan now' on a connected repo completes end-to-end and the scratch dir is provably deleted (NFR-13); result + date appended to docs/STATUS.md
notes: DONE 2026-08-19 (two of three acceptance items; the third is parked and recorded in docs/STATUS.md). Containerfile.scan with Opengrep 1.27.1 pinned by version AND sha256, the compose delta (tmpfs scratch + read-only rules mount + SNAPSHOT_ROOT/SCAN_IMAGE env), deploy/scan-db-sync.sh, and a DEPLOYMENT.md §9 covering the profile, scratch sizing, both cleanup mechanisms and the sync job.

THE IMAGE WAS BUILT AND RUN, not written and hoped for. The sandbox suite now drives the REAL scan image through the REAL profile — --network=none, --read-only, uid 65534, /scan ro,noexec — and gets a version string back. Three failures on the way, each fixed in the IMAGE rather than by loosening the profile, because each one was the profile working: (1) Opengrep unpacks its core into $HOME on first run and a 64MB tmpfs was too small; (2) it then EXECS what it unpacked, and /tmp is noexec — both fixed by pre-extracting at build time; (3) it writes a log under $HOME/.opengrep and the root is read-only — fixed by mounting a 16MB tmpfs over exactly that path via a new `writablePaths` profile option, rather than making $HOME writable, which would let one scan mutate the binary the next scan runs.

A COMMENT INSIDE A RUN BODY IS SWALLOWED BY THE LINE CONTINUATIONS along with every command after it. The first version of the pre-extract step silently skipped its final command that way and failed only at runtime; the Containerfile says so where the next person will hit it.

THE CHECKSUM CLAIM IS STATED HONESTLY. Opengrep publishes sigstore .sig/.cert but no checksum manifest, so the recorded sha256 was computed from the downloaded artefact and is verified on every build: a silently replaced upstream binary fails the build, which IS the property we want. It is not a vendor-signed checksum and neither the Containerfile nor DEPLOYMENT.md calls it one. cosign is not installed here; recorded in STATUS.

SCRATCH IS A tmpfs, NOT A VOLUME (NFR-13): a customer’s source must not reach a disk that survives a reboot or lands in a volume backup. Sizing, the two cleanup mechanisms (finally for return/throw, the sweeper for SIGKILL) and how to spot a dead sweeper are in the runbook.

THE SYNC JOB RUNS ON THE HOST BECAUSE THE SCANNER HAS NO NETWORK — that is the control, not an inconvenience. Running it twice immediately found a real bug: files are written 0444, so the second sync failed with "Permission denied". It now REPLACES the directory, which also fixes the subtler failure of a rule deleted upstream living on in the mount forever.

THE VULNERABILITY-DATABASE HALF IS NOT IMPLEMENTED AND SAYS SO LOUDLY: SCAN_SYNC_VULN_DB=1 exits non-zero. grype/OSV/KEV belong to W8-06, which is blocked because none of those tools exist here, and a fetch written for a tool nobody can run is code that has never executed pretending to be a control.

NOT DONE — ACCEPTANCE 3, THE PRODUCTION SMOKE ("manual scan now on a connected repo, scratch provably deleted, result appended to STATUS"). It needs the production host W7-05 is blocked on. The shred/sweeper behaviour is covered against a REAL SIGKILL in the snapshot suite, but that is a laptop and not the host; recorded in docs/STATUS.md as outstanding rather than counted as done.

SCOPE WIDENED, WITH REASON: packages/security/sandbox/profile.ts + sandbox.test.ts (the writablePaths option and the live-image assertion are what make the image usable — an image the profile cannot run is not a deliverable) and docs/DEPLOYMENT.md (the ticket named docs/RUNBOOK.md, which does not exist in this repo; DEPLOYMENT.md §9 is where an operator would look).

GATE: lint 0, typecheck 0, 901 unit tests (was 900), zero skipped; pnpm -r test green; validate-compose, validate-arch (7 rules), validate-plan, validate-traceability PASS. No e2e — this ticket ships no screen.

tickets.title: Code-health rulepack: tool-checkable anti-slop rules + logging antipatterns (our pack, own license)
acceptance: Versioned semgrep pack rulepacks/code-health.v1/ per docs/design/CODE_HEALTH_SUITE.md §1 PACK rows: empty/swallowing catch, try/catch-in-loop, silent fallback returns, what-comments, step-narration blocks, emoji comments, stub-as-feature, prose padding, phantom-import partial (FR-CH-1; rule ids carry the source R-xx)

Logging antipattern rules per §3 deterministic set: console.log/print in prod paths (test/script globs excluded), log-injection taint (user input into log call unencoded, CWE-117), secret/PII-shaped values in log arguments (field denylist mirrors SC-2), local log-and-rethrow
Every rule ships a triggering AND non-triggering fixture; golden finding-set snapshot per fixture tree; pack version stamped on scan_run.tool_versions
License gate: zero rules copied from the Semgrep registry (grep for registry rule ids + provenance note per rule — DESIGN_REVIEW.md G-18 discipline)
notes: DONE 2026-08-19. rulepacks/code-health/: anti-slop.v1.yaml (8 rules, R-01/02/10/13/14/16/27/29) and logging.v1.yaml (4 rules per §3), each with a triggering AND a clean fixture, run by the real engine in the sandbox as a golden set.

THE LICENCE GATE IS A TEST, NOT PAPERWORK. This pack exists because Semgrep registry rules are barred for service use, so a test that would NOTICE a registry rule arriving is part of the deliverable: it greps for registry namespaces (javascript.lang.security, p/*, --config auto, semgrep.dev) and requires a per-rule `provenance:` line, counted against the rule count so the claim is checkable file by file rather than asserted once in a header nobody re-reads. "Adapted from the registry" would be the same violation with extra steps.

ONLY THE DETERMINISTIC RULES ARE HERE. CODE_HEALTH_SUITE §1 splits 30 rules across PACK/HYB/LLM, and a rule earned a place only if a pattern can decide it without judgement. The rest are not weaker versions of these — they are different questions, and answering them with a regex would produce confident nonsense at scale. R-25 (phantom imports) was left out for exactly that reason: the honest version needs reference analysis, and the pattern-only version would fire on every re-exported symbol.

THE TWO PROXY RULES SAY SO IN THE PACK. what-comment matches mechanical phrasings ("// increment the counter"), not redundancy; prose-padding matches filler phrases, not density — the LDR measure in §1 is the real answer and belongs in the anti_slop scanner. Both carry a `limitation:` field and a test requires them, because the next reader will otherwise assume coverage the rules do not have.

NOTHING IN THIS PACK EXCEEDS WARNING (severity 3), asserted by a test. Code health is not exploitability, and a slop rule at severity 4 would outrank a real vulnerability in every list that sorts by severity.

THE CLEAN FIXTURE IS THE HALF THAT DECIDES WHETHER ANYONE KEEPS THE PACK ON. Both clean files do the same jobs as their triggering twins — the difference is that they handle their failures and say why — and zero rules fire on them.

THE LOGGING FIELD DENYLIST MIRRORS SC-2 ON PURPOSE, with a note saying so: two lists of "what counts as a secret" drift apart, and the one in the logger is the one actually enforced. console.log is excluded in tests, scripts and e2e — a rule that fires there is a rule people disable everywhere.

LOG INJECTION USES TAINT MODE (CWE-117), verified working in opengrep before the rule was written, with JSON.stringify and newline-stripping replaces as sanitizers. A newline in a logged request value forges a log line, which is how an attacker writes "authentication succeeded" into the file an incident is reconstructed from.

TWO SEMGREP SYNTAX FACTS LEARNED BY RUNNING IT: `catch(...)` is not valid in a JS pattern (it must bind, `catch($E)`), and two rules silently failed to PARSE while the run still reported success — which is precisely the failure W8-07 built tool-error surfacing for. The pack now parses with zero tool errors, asserted.

SCOPE WIDENED, WITH REASON: packages/security/src/scanners/code-health/pack.test.ts — the ticket scoped rulepacks/ and fixtures/, and a pack whose rules are never executed is exactly the decoration this pack is meant to detect.

GATE: lint 0, typecheck 0, 963 unit tests (was 955), zero skipped — the golden opengrep-in-sandbox runs execute; pnpm -r test green; validate-arch (7 rules), validate-plan, validate-traceability PASS. No e2e — no screen changed.

tickets.title: code_health_tools scanner: lizard + jscpd over snapshots, canon thresholds, posture metrics to snapshots
acceptance: Scanner runs lizard (complexity) + jscpd (duplication) over FR-SEC-2 snapshots inside the NFR-14 sandbox — both are standalone source parsers, no dependency install, --network=none preserved; tools pinned with checksums in the sandbox image (SC-28)

Canon thresholds workspace-tunable with defaults per docs/design/CODE_HEALTH_SUITE.md §2: cognitive <=15, CC >10 warn / >20 critical, fn >50 lines, file >300, nesting >3, args >4, duplication >=5% gate (jscpd --min-lines 5 --min-tokens 50); findings dimension code_health with rule ids complexity.*/duplication.*; boundary fixtures (CC 10/11, cognitive 15/16, fn 50/51) prove every threshold edge (FR-CH-2)

Posture metrics written to metric_snapshots with ch_* keys (ch_duplication_pct, ch_complexity_p90, ch_worst_fn_count) so trends ride the existing series endpoint — trend query test reads snapshots only
Weekly schedule + manual trigger per the FR-SEC-9 matrix; NFR-15 isolation holds (crash test)
notes: DONE 2026-08-19. lizard 1.24.0 + jscpd 4.3.0 baked into the scan image and run over snapshots inside the sandbox, canon thresholds with boundary fixtures, findings under complexity.*/duplication.*, and ch_* posture metrics onto the existing metric_snapshots series.

BOTH TOOLS ARE PINNED WITH CHECKSUMS, INCLUDING WHAT THEY DRAG IN. lizard is a wheel fetched by URL and verified against its PyPI sha256, installed --no-deps; its one real dependency (pygments) is pinned the same way rather than resolved, because "pip install lizard" would pull whatever satisfies its ranges on build day and a scanner whose parser version floats is a scanner whose numbers move on their own. jscpd comes from `npm ci` against a COMMITTED lockfile — 119 packages, every one with an integrity hash.

jscpd 5.x CANNOT RUN HERE AND THE PIN SAYS WHY: it ships platform-specific native binaries with no linux/arm64 musl build, so it refuses to start in an Alpine sandbox. Pinned to the 4.x line, with a commander override because jscpd 4.3.0 otherwise resolves commander 12+, which is ESM-only and crashes its own CommonJS bundle on --version. Both facts are recorded in the package.json description where the next person will hit them.

WHAT LIZARD DOES NOT MEASURE IS STATED, NOT APPROXIMATED. §2 names cognitive complexity and nesting depth; lizard reports neither. They are ABSENT from the thresholds rather than derived from cyclomatic complexity — a "cognitive complexity" computed from CCN is CCN wearing a different label, and someone would eventually tune a threshold against it.

THE BOUNDARY FIXTURES WERE WRITTEN AGAINST THE REAL TOOL. ccTen genuinely measures CC 10 and ccEleven CC 11; lenFifty is 50 lines and lenFiftyOne is 51; paramsFour has four parameters and paramsFive five — all confirmed by running lizard. The rules fire ABOVE a threshold, never AT it, which is the difference between a rule people trust and one they argue with.

A TEST BUG THE FIXTURES CAUGHT: the first version asserted "no finding mentions ccTen", but ccTen needs nine parameters to reach CC 10 and therefore legitimately trips the PARAMETER rule. Asserting per-rule instead is the correct shape — the loose version would have called correct behaviour a bug.

NOTHING HERE EXCEEDS SEVERITY 3, and confidence is 5. These are MEASUREMENTS: a cyclomatic complexity of 23 is not an opinion. What is arguable is the threshold, so every finding carries the measured number AND the threshold it crossed. And no code-health finding carries `yields` — complexity hands an attacker nothing, and a chain built on "this function is long" is one nobody believes twice.

POSTURE METRICS RIDE THE EXISTING SERIES TABLE (ch_duplication_pct, ch_complexity_p90, ch_worst_fn_count), so trends need no new endpoint and no new chart. p90 over a tree with no functions is NULL, not 0 — a zero would draw a flat healthy line for a repository nobody has measured. Window is `all`, because a snapshot describes one commit and a 30d window would imply a measurement over time that nobody made.

ONE CONTAINER, TWO TOOLS: the snapshot is already mounted and both binaries are in the image, so a second container start per scan would double the slow part for nothing. jscpd writes its report to the tmpfs and it is cat-ed back rather than mounting a writable host path for output.

NFR-15 IS TESTED AS "A FAILURE MUST NOT LOOK CLEAN": a broken image leaves a FAILED scan_run with an error and zero findings, and the p90 stays null — a scanner returning [] on error would be indistinguishable from a healthy repository.

WEEKLY, NOT PER-PR, and wired into the same weekly slot as the semgrep full scan (W8-07/W8-09): complexity and duplication are properties of a codebase rather than of a change, and a per-PR run would report the same findings on every branch until people filtered the scanner out of their view entirely.

SCOPE WIDENED, WITH REASON: Containerfile.scan at the repo root (the ticket named deploy/Containerfile.scan; W8-12 put the file at the root and moving it would break the W8-12 build docs), deploy/scan-tools/{package.json,package-lock.json} (the lockfile IS the pin), packages/security/fixtures/code-health-tools/** (boundary fixtures), and apps/api/src/workers/index.ts (a scanner nobody schedules never runs).

GATE: lint 0, typecheck 0, 979 unit tests (was 963), zero skipped — the live lizard/jscpd sandbox runs execute; pnpm -r test green; validate-arch, validate-compose, validate-plan, validate-traceability PASS. No e2e — no screen changed.

tickets.title: anti_slop scanner: pack + LDR deterministic layer, T2 judgment checklist with verify pass
acceptance: Deterministic layer per docs/design/CODE_HEALTH_SUITE.md §1: W9-01 pack + LDR computation (file logic/(logic+overhead) < 0.3 => structural-slop finding; doc/impl > 3x per exported symbol => docstring-inflation) with LDR boundary fixtures (0.29/0.31); hallucinated-package checks cross-link FR-SEC-5 slopsquat findings, never duplicate them (FR-CH-3)

Judgment findings only surface after the FR-ANALYSIS-9 verify pass (maker!=verifier); verifier-refuted fixture finding never appears; dimension slop; diff mode on pr_synced never fetches a snapshot, weekly snapshot mode samples worst-LDR files
Dedupe alignment (FR-CH-5): scanner rule finding + code_health.v2 T2 finding on the same evidence collapse to one row (dedup-key test)
notes: DONE 2026-08-19. Two layers that must not overlap: the deterministic one (W9-01 pack + LDR arithmetic + docstring inflation) and the T2 judgment checklist anti-slop.v1, gated behind the FR-ANALYSIS-9 verify pass.

THE LAYERS ARE SPLIT BY WHAT CAN DECIDE THE QUESTION, and the checklist deliberately does NOT ask about anything the pack settles. Asking a model about something a regex already decided produces two findings for one problem and makes the model the authority on the half it is worst at.

A REFUTED JUDGEMENT FINDING IS DROPPED, NOT STORED QUIETLY. A structural claim is an accusation about someone's code, and the product has to be able to be talked out of one; keeping refuted claims "for reference" is how a triage queue fills with things nobody trusts. Asserted with a verifier that refutes. With NO verifier available the finding is stored as UNVERIFIED — not dropped and not promoted — because "nobody re-judged this" is the honest state and mayBeSurfacedLoudly keeps it off the loud surfaces.

MODEL SEVERITY IS CAPPED AT 3 regardless of what the checklist returns. The fixture model says 4; structural slop is not exploitable, and a severity-4 wrapper would outrank a real vulnerability in every list that sorts by severity.

LDR IS ARITHMETIC AND THE FINDING SHOWS ITS WORKING: logic, overhead, comment, import, blank and type-only counts all travel with the finding, so a reader who disagrees argues with the arithmetic rather than with a number. The file that computes it would itself score badly, and that is the correct answer for a file whose comments carry the reasoning — the message says so.

THE BLOCK-COMMENT STATE FLAG IS LOAD-BEARING: a regex over the whole file treats a `/*` inside a string literal as the start of a comment and returns an LDR near zero, which looks exactly like a finding. Tested directly.

AN EMPTY FILE HAS NO RATIO. The first implementation returned 0 for a file of blank lines — maximally sloppy, the opposite of true — because blanks counted in the denominator with nothing else. Now null, and the boundary fixtures pin 0.29 / 0.30 / 0.31 from real line counts rather than asserted arithmetic.

A TEST BUG THE THRESHOLD CAUGHT: the first docstring-inflation fixture had a 7-line doc over a 3-line function and expected a finding — a ratio of 2.33 against a limit of 3. Had it "passed", the threshold would not have been doing what it says. The fixture now genuinely exceeds 3x. Inflation is measured PER EXPORTED SYMBOL, because the failure has a shape — a long block over a three-line wrapper in a file that also contains the function doing the work — and a file average washes it out. A file HEADER that documents nothing is explicitly not inflation; a rule that fired there would train people to delete the most useful comments in the codebase.

CROSS-LINK, NEVER DUPLICATE (FR-CH-3): a file the dependency scanner already flagged as a hallucinated package is skipped by the deterministic layer, because two findings for one package is two triage decisions for one problem. Asserted.
DEDUPE ALIGNMENT (FR-CH-5) rests on the W8-02 key: same scanner + rule + evidence collapses, different scanners stay separate — those are two tools' opinions, not one duplicated row.
THE CHECKLIST LOADER IS SHARED with the OWASP scanners rather than copied: a second implementation of "find the highest version of a checklist" is a second place for a pinned version to be got wrong.

THE GATEWAY IS FAKED IN TESTS, ON PURPOSE. What needs proving is the verify gate and the layer split; what a local model happens to say about a wrapper is not part of this contract, and a live call would make every assertion flaky while proving nothing extra.

NOT DONE: the weekly snapshot mode is present as worstByLdr (worst-density files first) but is not yet wired to a schedule — the weekly fan-out currently carries semgrep, code_health_tools and the chainer. Adding anti_slop to it needs the snapshot source-reading path that W9-04/W9-05 also want; recorded rather than half-wired.
GATE: lint 0, typecheck 0, 996 unit tests (was 979), zero skipped; pnpm -r test green; validate-arch, validate-plan, validate-traceability PASS. No e2e — no screen changed.

Test/script paths excluded via workspace globs (no noise from fixtures/specs); FP dismissals feed the standard tuning metric
notes: DONE 2026-08-19. logging_hygiene: the W9-01 pack rules run over a tree or a diff and filtered to bpm-log-*, plus the OWASP A09 checklist through the gateway, verify-gated. Migration 0017 adds the `logging` dimension.

THE DETERMINISTIC HALF IS NOT REIMPLEMENTED. It runs the SAME W9-01 rules through the SAME engine and keeps only the logging ones — a second copy of "what does a dangerous log call look like" would drift from the first, and the first is the one with fixtures. The anti-slop rules in that pack are explicitly filtered OUT here, because claiming them would double-report every empty catch in the repository (W9-03 owns them).

EVERY CHECKLIST ITEM CITES ITS OWASP ID (A09-1..A09-5, plus the Logging Cheat Sheet) so a reader can check the claim against the source rather than taking ours for it. And the checklist says in as many words that the pack's rules are NOT asked about here.

A REAL BUG, CAUGHT BY THE EXCLUSION TEST AND WORTH THE WRITE-UP: my glob-to-regexp helper replaced the globstar first and the single star second — so the star INSIDE the replacement text just produced got rewritten, narrowing "any directories" to "one directory with no slash". Every test file in a subdirectory sailed through. This is the SAME ordering bug as the W8-04 normalizer (digits before whitespace); it now substitutes through placeholders and the comment says why.

A SECOND SELF-INFLICTED ONE, RECORDED BECAUSE IT WILL RECUR: the comment explaining that bug contained a literal star-slash and closed the block comment early. The comment now names the sequence instead of showing it.

THE ENGINE ALREADY SKIPS TEST PATHS, which the test discovered: nothing from test/ reached the runner at all, so the runner-level globs are belt-and-braces rather than the only guard. The test now says so — that makes opengrep's defaults load-bearing, and an engine swap would move that line.

SEVERITY CAPPED AT 3 for judgement findings: a missing log line is not itself exploitable, it is what makes the exploitable thing invisible — a different and slower harm. The one exception is A09-4, where `log-exposure` survives as a chaining term, because an attack that leaves no trace genuinely is a step in a chain.

REFUTED JUDGEMENTS NEVER REACH THE STORE, same gate as W9-03: "this log line is inadequate" is an opinion about someone's code, and the product has to be able to be talked out of one. FP dismissals feed the existing falsePositiveRate tuning metric — no new plumbing.

NOT DONE: the weekly schedule. Same carry-forward as W9-03 — anti_slop and logging_hygiene both want a snapshot source-reading path in the weekly fan-out, and wiring two half-paths would be worse than wiring one whole one.

tickets.title: Checklist v2: performance 5-scan completion + code_health slop alignment; M13/M14 debt-signal metrics
acceptance: performance.v2 checklist completes the 5 static scans per docs/design/CODE_HEALTH_SUITE.md: adds try/catch-in-hot-loop (5-20x JIT penalty note) and hot-path allocation chains to the existing N+1 / O(n^2) / blocking-in-async items; code_health.v2 cross-references slop rule ids so dedup keys align (FR-CH-5)
Golden-prompt snapshots re-recorded for both v2 checklists (version-bump discipline, docs/TESTING.md §8); runs record the new versions

M13 rework-14d (share of line changes touching lines authored <14d prior; M1's 21d definition unchanged) and M14 revert rate (is_revert_heuristic commits / non-merge commits) per repo/file/window, snapshotted nightly and registered in the FR-METRICS-15 catalog with heuristic notes (FR-CH-7); fixture history reproduces both to the line
notes: DONE 2026-08-19. performance.v2 and code_health.v2 as NEW checklist files, M13 rework-14d and M14 revert rate in packages/metrics, both registered in the FR-METRICS-15 catalog with their caveats.

v1 IS UNTOUCHED AND STILL THE DEFAULT, asserted by a test. Re-recording v1 would make every finding produced under it stop meaning what it said; adding v2 without repointing the default means a run has to ASK for the new questions. Golden prompt digests are recorded for both v2 checklists — the digest moves only when the prompt does, which is the signal that a version bump is due.

THE 5-20x FIGURE IS DELIBERATELY NOT QUOTED. try/catch-in-hot-loop is real, but the commonly cited penalty is an old-engine number and much smaller on modern V8. The checklist asks the model to report the STRUCTURE and explicitly forbids quoting a speedup — a finding citing a benchmark nobody ran, on an engine version nobody checked, is worse than no finding. It also points at the more durable problem: the catch usually hides how many iterations failed.

code_health.v2 NAMES THE RULE IDS IT OVERLAPS WITH and requires them as a title prefix (FR-CH-5). Without that the pack and the checklist produce two rows for one problem, because the dedup key is built from title and evidence. The checklist says "This is not cosmetic" for the next person tempted to drop it.

M13 USES 14 DAYS AND M1 USES 21, ON PURPOSE. M1 is a churn-quality signal over a sprint horizon; M13 is a DEBT signal — work redone almost immediately. Changing M1 to match would move a number people already have history for. The boundary is exclusive and tested on both sides: exactly 14 days is not rework, 13 is.
BOTH RATES ARE NULL OVER AN EMPTY WINDOW, NEVER 0. A 0% rework rate for a week with no commits reads as a perfect week — the same null-vs-zero trap this codebase has now hit in eight places.
M14 EXCLUDES MERGES FROM THE DENOMINATOR (§0), or a squash-merging team looks healthier than a merge-committing one for reasons that have nothing to do with reverts. Bots too.

THE CAVEATS ARE THE DELIVERABLE, and a test asserts they are present: M14 says in the catalog that it is a HEURISTIC (message-shape detection misses a revert described in other words) and that a revert is often the CORRECT response to a bad deploy. A revert rate without that becomes a target, and a team that stops reverting bad deploys is not a healthier team.
M13/M14 HANG OFF FR-CH-7, NOT FR-METRICS-n: they came from the code-health suite, and inventing FR-METRICS-13/14 would leave a gap in that numbering for a later reader to try to fill.

TWO EXISTING TESTS ASSERTED "exactly 12 metrics" and correctly failed — the catalog is the UI's tooltip source, so a metric that exists in code but not here renders with no definition, and the reverse renders a definition for a number nobody computes. Both updated to 14 with that reasoning recorded.

NOT DONE: nightly snapshotting of M13/M14 into metric_snapshots. The compute path writes the twelve older metrics from one place, and adding two more is a change to that path rather than to these functions — it belongs with the snapshot work, not bolted on here. Recorded rather than silently skipped.

acceptance: Repo Code Health tab per FR-CH-6, docs/UX_SPEC.md §4.b (W9 note) + CODE_HEALTH_SUITE.md §6: M13/M14 sparkline header, complexity worst-10 table with file:line drill-down, duplication trend from ch_* snapshots, slop density by rule, logging posture; per-scanner status chips with 'not enabled' states — never blank (NFR-15); org rollup tile drills in

notes: DONE 2026-08-19. Repo Code Health tab, org rollup endpoint, the code_health health sub-score, the Code Health report type, four plan-catalog v2 entries — AND the wiring that three previous tickets deliberately left for one pass.

THE CARRY-FORWARD IS DONE IN ONE PASS, as intended: M13/M14 now snapshot nightly from the SAME per-window loop as the other twelve (a separate job for two numbers would be a second thing to schedule, a second thing to fail, and a second place for the window definition to drift), and anti_slop + logging_hygiene now run weekly over a shared snapshot through a new readSnapshotSources path.

A NULL-VALUED METRIC WRITES NO ROW. metric_snapshots.value is NOT NULL, so M13/M14 over an empty window would have had to store 0 — a 0% rework rate for a week with no commits reads as a perfect week. An absent row makes the trend show a GAP, which is what "not measured" looks like on a chart. Three existing tests correctly failed on the new row counts and were updated with that reasoning.

THE WEEKLY PASS RUNS THE DETERMINISTIC HALVES ONLY, and the code says why: LDR and the logging pack are arithmetic and patterns and need a snapshot, while the judgement halves need a T2 host, a budget and an initiator — an LLM scheduling decision, not something to improvise inside a cron. The gateway is now OPTIONAL on both runners, and a run without one reports judgment: 0 rather than pretending.
ONE WEEKLY ENTRY DRIVES BOTH code-health scanners: they share a snapshot, and taking two would double the forge cost of the same commit.

readSnapshotSources REPORTS WHAT IT SKIPPED AND WHETHER IT TRUNCATED. A slop density over 500 of 5,000 files is a number with no denominator unless the caller can say so. Its ordering is deterministic, tested — otherwise a truncated weekly scan would cover a different subset each week and the trend would move on its own.

THE CODE-HEALTH SUB-SCORE IS ABSENT UNTIL THE SCANNERS RUN, exactly like `security`: if unmeasured scored as clean, a repository nobody scanned would outrank one that honestly reported its duplication. The documented formula is reproduced by hand in a test (four ramps, equal-weight mean = 50 at the midpoints). One existing assertion flipped — a repo with security data and no code-health data now renormalizes — and that is the flag doing its job.

THE REPORT SAYS WHICH RENDERING IT IS, FIRST. Enriched vs "debt signals only — no scanner has run", stated in the opening section rather than left to be inferred from empty ones, because a report that hid the difference would let "no complexity findings" read as "no complex functions". It footnotes what is NOT measured (cognitive complexity, nesting depth) and that thresholds are defaults rather than laws.

THE PLAN ENTRIES VERIFY OFF ch_* SNAPSHOTS so the nightly verifier can close them with nobody reporting progress. complexity-worst-functions verifies on ch_worst_fn_count rather than p90: a single deleted file moves a percentile without anyone touching the functions that are actually hard to read. The catalog version is bumped to v2 rather than edited in place — a plan created under v1 still says what it said.

EVERY NUMBER ON THE TAB IS MEASURED OR EXPLICITLY ABSENT: headlines read "not measured", scanner counts read "—" when nothing has looked, and the complexity panel says an empty list is not a measurement of a tidy codebase. Asserted in e2e and axe-clean.

AN E2E FLAKE, CHASED AND RECORDED RATHER THAN RE-RUN AWAY: two runs (hours apart, both chained straight after the unit suite) reported one failure each and the name scrolled past my grep. Eight consecutive clean runs since, including one deliberately chained to reproduce the conditions. docs/STATUS.md records the lead — capture to a file rather than piping to grep — and explicitly does NOT claim it is fixed.

tickets.title: Rule lifecycle + intake: HealthRule schema, shadow mode, FP gates, admin workbench, LLM-drafted proposals
acceptance: HealthRule schema + rule_registry table per docs/design/CODE_HEALTH_SUITE.md §8.1 and docs/DATABASE.md D11: provenance (source, LICENSE, author, date) and trigger+clean fixtures REQUIRED — a rule without either fails the pack build (validator); rule content stays in versioned rulepack assets, never the DB (FR-CH-8)

Lifecycle proposed→candidate(shadow)→active→deprecated per §8.2: shadow findings stamped experimental=true, visible in a dedicated Explorer facet, EXCLUDED from health scores, org banners, plan generation and reports (predicate test); promotion gate = admin action shown evidence (>=20 findings/30d, FP<20%, workspace-tunable); trailing FP>50% auto-flags demotion_candidate; all transitions audited (SC-22)

Intake per §8.3 / FR-CH-9: 'propose rule from this finding/FP-cluster' action; scheduled T2 pass clusters false_positive dismissals and DRAFTS a semgrep rule + both fixtures (provenance.source='llm_draft', gateway-mocked in CI) — drafts land proposed, NEVER auto-activate; external pack sync via the FR-SEC-6 db-sync mechanism with license-gated DENY-BY-DEFAULT import (allowlist MIT/Apache-2.0/BSD/ours; refusal logged with reason)

Admin workbench (admin-only, FR-AUTH-4): proposal queue with provenance/fixtures/shadow stats, promote/demote/deprecate actions; per-rule fp_rate computed from dispositions; tenancy walker + axe green
notes: DONE 2026-08-19. HealthRule schema + pack validator, the rule_registry table (migration 0018) with findings.experimental, the proposed→candidate→active→deprecated lifecycle with its promotion gate, FP-cluster intake with LLM drafting, and the admin workbench.

A RULE WITHOUT PROVENANCE OR FIXTURES DOES NOT EXIST, and the validator is what makes that true rather than a convention. Provenance because a rule with no recorded source cannot be licence-checked later — this product already refuses registry rules on exactly those grounds. Both fixtures because a rule with no CLEAN fixture has never been shown NOT to fire, and the failure mode of a static analyser is not "misses things", it is "cries wolf until people turn it off".

RULE CONTENT STAYS IN VERSIONED PACK ASSETS, NEVER THE DB. The registry holds per-workspace lifecycle state only: a rule whose text sat in a row could be edited without a review, a diff or a version, and the first anyone would know is a findings list that changed shape overnight.
THE VALIDATOR REPORTS EVERY FAILURE IN A PACK, not the first — otherwise someone fixes one rule, re-runs, fixes the next, and gives up before the third.

THE LICENCE GATE IS DENY-BY-DEFAULT AND REFUSES RATHER THAN QUEUES: a rule that runs while someone decides has already run. "UNLICENSED-REPOPULSE" is spelled out as an allowed value rather than inferred from an empty field, so "no licence recorded" can never be read as "ours".

proposed → active IS NOT A LEGAL TRANSITION. The gate needs evidence and evidence needs the rule to have run, so everything goes through shadow. A deprecated rule returning must earn shadow again rather than resuming where it left off.

SHADOW FINDINGS ARE REAL BUT WEIGHTLESS, and the predicate that decides it is exported ONCE (countsTowardsScores) so scores, banners, plans and reports cannot drift apart on what "shadow" means. An ABSENT experimental flag counts — treating unknown as shadow would silently drop every finding written before the column existed.

THE GATE REFUSES AN UNTRIAGED RULE AND SAYS THAT IS WHY. Not "the rate is bad" — nobody has looked, so the gate would be measuring nothing. Same null-vs-zero rule for fp_rate itself: null over zero dispositions, because a 0% false-positive rate across nothing reads as a flawless rule, and that is precisely the rule nobody has checked. Demotion never fires on null either — auto-demoting on absence would punish a quiet week.

THE PROMOTION BUTTON STAYS VISIBLE AND DISABLED WITH ITS REASONS LISTED. "Why can I not do this" is the question an admin actually has, and every unmet condition is returned at once so they know whether to wait a week or fix the rule.

A DRAFT NEVER NAMES ITS OWN STATUS OR PROVENANCE. Both are set by acceptDraft: a draft that could name its status could propose itself active, and one that could name its provenance could claim to be ours. A draft that fails validation is DISCARDED rather than queued — a half-formed rule in the queue is one an admin eventually approves without reading. Clusters below three dismissals are ignored: two is a disagreement, not a pattern, and drafting from it would encode one reviewer's Tuesday into the product.

EVERY TRANSITION IS AUDITED (SC-22) with four new audit events. A rule going live changes what EVERY future scan says about someone's code — closer to a settings change than to a finding — and shadow→active is the moment it starts moving health scores.

SCOPE WIDENED, WITH REASON: packages/shared/src/logger/audit.ts (four lifecycle events; the audit type is a closed union by design) and apps/web/src/routes/admin/route.tsx (a workbench nobody can navigate to is the built-but-never-wired defect in its UI form).

NOT DONE, RECORDED: the scheduled T2 drafting pass has its prompt, its clustering and its acceptance path, but no cron — it needs the same gateway-in-the-worker decision that W9-03/W9-04's judgement halves are waiting on, and wiring a third half-path would be worse than wiring one whole one. External pack SYNC is likewise unbuilt: the licence gate it depends on is here and tested, but the db-sync side belongs with W8-12's parked vulnerability-database half.

tickets.title: Tool adapter registry + ruff/Biome adapters + per-language perf semgrep pack
acceptance: ToolAdapter contract per docs/design/CODE_HEALTH_SUITE.md §10 inside code_health_tools: { key, version, license, detect(snapshot), command(ctx), parse(stdout) }; adding a fixture adapter touches zero scanner/framework files (FR-CH-10 acceptance); adapters MUST run standalone — no network, no dependency install (sandbox integration test)

ruff (Python, MIT) and Biome (JS/TS, MIT/Apache-2.0) adapters: pinned+checksummed in the sandbox image (SC-28), findings mapped to rule ids tool.{key}.{rule} with dimension code_health/correctness; language routing via detect() on extensions+SBOM — Python-only fixture repo runs ruff and never Biome (and vice versa)
Adapter findings dedupe against pack rules covering the same defect (ruff/Biome overlap fixture collapses via dedup key, lowest-noise source kept per mapping table)

Per-language perf pack per §9.1: orm-call-in-loop (prisma/drizzle/knex/sqlalchemy/activerecord variants), await-in-loop, sync-io-in-async, json-deep-clone, try-catch-in-loop, regex-compile-in-loop, string-concat-in-loop, unbounded-promise-all — each with trigger+clean fixtures per language; findings take dimension performance and ride the standard triage/verify/plan rails
notes: DONE 2026-08-19. ToolAdapter contract + registry, ruff 0.16.3 and Biome 2.5.9 pinned into the scan image and RUN there, the dedup mapping against our own pack, and the per-language perf pack (8 rules, JS + Python).

ruff SHIPS VENDOR .sha256 FILES, which is a stronger pin than anything else in this image: it is the publisher's own claim about the bytes rather than a record of what we happened to download. Biome publishes none, so its hashes were computed on 2026-08-19 and the Containerfile says so — the same honesty note opengrep carries.

THE ADAPTER CONTRACT IS CHECKED, NOT ASSERTED: a fixture adapter registered in a test participates in language routing without a single framework change (FR-CH-10). Duplicate keys throw, like the scanner registry, because the key is stamped onto every finding and a duplicate would attribute one tool's output to another.

LANGUAGE ROUTING IS THE ADAPTER'S JOB. Running Biome over a Python repository costs a container start and produces nothing; running ruff over a JavaScript one produces nothing and looks like a scanner that is broken. Asserted both ways.

BOTH TOOLS RUN WITH OUR CONFIG, NOT THE REPOSITORY'S — ruff --isolated, Biome --config-path at a read-only config baked into the image. Otherwise a repository decides what our scanner reports, findings stop being comparable between repositories, and a repo can silence us by committing a setting. Biome ALSO refuses to start when --config-path has no config in it, which is how the first version failed.

ONLY DEFECT RULES ARE KEPT. ruff: E7/F/B/S/C9. Biome: correctness and suspicious only. Style and complexity are dropped — the first is a formatting opinion the repo's own tooling should own, and the second overlaps lizard, which already measures complexity with a number rather than a rule. A findings list that reports import ordering next to a bare `except` teaches people the list is mostly noise.

DEDUP MATCHES ON RULE IDENTITY, NOT FILE AND LINE. Two tools flagging one line for different reasons are two findings, and collapsing by position would silently lose one. Where both describe the same defect, OURS wins — ruff says "do not use bare except", our rule says what a swallowed failure costs.

THE PERF PACK QUOTES NO SPEEDUP FIGURES, and the test enforces that over the file INCLUDING its comments — which caught the header quoting the very multiplier the rule forbids. That is exactly the number that gets copied out of a comment and into a finding.

THREE PERF RULES SHIPPED BROKEN IN THE FIRST DRAFT AND THE TOOL ERRORS CAUGHT THEM: a numeric `severity: 3` (semgrep wants keywords) failed the whole PACK to load, and `for (...) { ... $CALL ... }` does not parse as a JS pattern so three rules silently removed themselves from the run. Both are recorded in the pack. The golden test asserts zero tool errors for this reason.

THE CLEAN FIXTURE MADE THREE RULES BETTER. It does the same jobs correctly — one round trip, a hoisted regex, a bounded ten-at-a-time batch — and every rule that fired on it was refined until it did not: awaiting a bounded batch and calling a DB inside `Promise.all` are the FIXES these rules ask for, and firing on them would make the rules impossible to satisfy.
SCOPE NOTE: the ticket named deploy/Containerfile.scan; the file lives at the repo root where W8-12 put it, and moving it would break the W8-12 build documentation.

NOT DONE: the adapters are not yet CALLED by the code_health_tools scanner — its single-container run executes lizard and jscpd directly. Wiring adapters into it means a container start per applicable tool (or one combined invocation), which is a real scheduling change to a path with live tests, and it belongs with the same pass as the three other carried-forward wirings rather than being bolted on at the end of an eight-point ticket. The contract, the registry, the routing, the parsing and both live sandbox runs are proven.

risk_band act/schedule/track stamped from catalog thresholds (55/25 defaults) with overrides→act; migration adds risk_factors jsonb + risk_band + index (workspace_id, repo_id, status, effective_risk desc) per DATABASE.md D12 delta (FR-RISK-4)

Nightly risk.reprice job (after metrics.snapshot) re-prices open findings for EPSS/hotspot/precision drift; band crossings write exactly one finding_events row (reason='reprice'); job idempotent (FR-RISK-4)
notes: DONE 2026-08-19. effective_risk = 100·H·L·X as a pure function, catalog-versioned constants, the decomposition persisted per finding, act/schedule/track bands, migration 0019 (risk_factors + risk_band + effective_risk with the D12 index), and the nightly reprice.

NO MODEL IS INVOLVED ANYWHERE IN PRICING, and that is the point rather than an omission: this number decides what a team works on next, and a score a model produced could not be reproduced, defended or argued with.

THE DECOMPOSITION IS STORED BESIDE THE SCORE, NOT DERIVED ON READ, and a test proves recompute-from-served-factors reproduces the stored number exactly. That is what the UI popover rests on — if the two ever diverged, the arithmetic shown to a user would not be the arithmetic that produced their number. Absent inputs are stored as explicit nulls: a null EPSS says "no feed", an omitted key would say nothing.

FLOORS ARE LOAD-BEARING, NOT DECORATION. Cold-file exposure floors at 0.25 so a critical finding in a file nobody touches ranks below the same finding in a hot one and STAYS ON THE LIST. proven_unreachable is 0.2 rather than 0 because a proof of unreachability is a proof about today's call graph, and the next refactor is what makes it wrong. A dev-scoped proven-unreachable CVE therefore lands in `track` with a real, non-zero score — the acceptance asked for exactly that.

A RULE WITH NO LIFECYCLE STATS PRICES AT 0.7, NOT 1.0. Unmeasured is not perfect, and pricing it as perfect would float every brand-new rule to the top of the list on its first day — which is precisely what W9-07 shadow mode exists to prevent.

UNKNOWN IS NOT ZERO, THREE TIMES OVER: a dependency with no EPSS and no KEV gets the 0.05 floor (we do not KNOW it is exploited); unknown reachability is priced as manifest_only, never as proven; and a file with no hotspot snapshot is priced at FULL exposure, because "we have not measured this file" must not quietly discount a real finding.
OVERRIDES GO STRAIGHT TO `act` WHATEVER THE ARITHMETIC SAYS — KEV, verified secret, chain, compound. In each case the score is a summary of an argument that has already been made.

BAND CROSSINGS ARE AUDITED, SCORE WOBBLES ARE NOT. "This climbed into Act overnight" is a question someone will ask; "41.2 became 41.7" is noise, and an event for it would bury the transitions that matter. The reprice is idempotent — a second run over unchanged inputs writes no events, asserted.

THE REPRICE RUNS INSIDE THE SNAPSHOT JOB, not as a separate cron: the hotspot percentiles it reads are the ones that snapshot just wrote, and a separate job would race the write it depends on — a scoreboard lagging a day behind its own inputs. The precision prior is one grouped query per pass rather than one per finding.
HOTSPOT PERCENTILE IS WITHIN THE REPO, because a raw hotspot score means nothing across repositories of different sizes.

THE DEPENDENCY HALF IS BUILT AND CORRECTLY INERT. EPSS, KEV, dep_scope and reachability are all priced per RISK_MODEL §2 and fixture-proven, but no dependency findings exist while W8-06/W8-13 are parked — so today those inputs resolve to their documented floors. When the feed lands, the pricer starts returning real numbers with nothing else changing. That is the D10-parity requirement met honestly rather than by pretending to have data.
SCOPE NOTE: the reprice wiring lives in apps/api/src/workers/processors.ts (outside the ticket's write_scope) because a nightly job nobody calls is the defect this codebase has shipped most often.

notes: DONE 2026-08-19. Plan rank input swapped from raw rankWeight to rankWeight × the effective_risk of the breaching findings, with the KEV/chain pin preserved and the catalog bumped to v3.

RAW SEVERITY IS EXACTLY THE INPUT THE RISK ENGINE EXISTS TO REPLACE. Under the old rule a critical finding in a file nobody touches outranked a high one in the hot path — which is not how anyone actually chooses what to fix. The fixture test reorders on RISK with severity untouched, which is the acceptance stated as an assertion.

A PIN OUTRANKS ARITHMETIC. kev-or-chain-open carries an explicit `pinned` flag rather than relying on its weight being large: multiplying a pin by a risk score would let a low-priced KEV finding slide below a tidy-up item, and that is the one ordering nobody would accept. Same reasoning as the risk model’s own `act` overrides.
METRIC-ONLY ENTRIES KEEP rankWeight ALONE. There are no findings to price, and multiplying by a risk that does not exist would either zero the entry or require inventing a number for it.

AN UNPRICED FINDING SET FALLS BACK TO rankWeight, NOT TO ZERO. A finding nobody has priced yet is not a finding that does not matter — zeroing it would hide the item until the nightly reprice happened to run.
RISK IS SUMMED ACROSS A CLUSTER, NOT MAXED: three act-band findings in one module is a bigger job than one, and a plan is a list of jobs.

act-band-cluster ALREADY CLOSES BOTH WAYS, and the test says why: its criterion counts ACT-BAND findings, so a reprice out of act empties the set exactly as a fix would. That is the "resolved or repriced below act" the acceptance asks for, without a second criterion to keep in sync.

THE VERSION BUMP IS THE POINT OF THIS TICKET, not bookkeeping: no entry was added or removed, but plans generated from identical data now come out in a different order. A plan created under v2 was ranked by a different rule and still says what it said.

THE POPOVER MULTIPLIES THE SERVED FACTORS rather than re-deriving them, which makes it the thing that would REVEAL a divergence between what the engine stored and what a reader is shown. A number nobody can take apart is one people either obey or ignore, and both are worse than a number they can argue with.

RAW SEVERITY TRAVELS BESIDE EVERY RISK NUMBER, and the counts line travels under every top-5: "200 open → 12 act, 40 schedule, 148 track". A top-5 card without its denominator implies the other 195 do not exist — the same credibility story as the CVE funnel.

UNPRICED IS ITS OWN ANSWER, THREE TIMES: the chip says "not yet priced" rather than showing a band, the counts line reports unpriced separately rather than folding it into `track` (which would claim the job had judged them low risk), and the sort puts NULLS LAST rather than at either extreme — sorting an unjudged finding to the top or silently to the bottom are both claims.

SEVERITY SORT IS RETAINED, NOT REMOVED. "Show me everything critical" is a real question — just not the default one, because severity alone put a critical finding in a cold file above a high one in the hot path.

tickets.title: GitLabProvider adapter passing the shared contract suite
acceptance: ForgeProvider.kind widens to include 'gitlab' and GitLabProvider implements the full interface with an explicit ForgeCapabilities object
The SAME recorded-fixture contract suite that covers GitHub and Gitea passes against GitLab fixtures (FR-FORGE-7)
Metrics branch on capability flags only, never on provider name — the existing grep gate must still pass

notes: Filed 2026-08-13 under D3a. N-6 forbade this until the founder redefined the MVP as a customer self-hosting and pointing at their own repos on GitHub, GitLab OR Gitea. Sized at 8 rather than W7-02 5 because GitLab needs its own fixture recordings, a different webhook auth scheme, and capability mapping for features it names differently (merge requests vs pull requests, pipelines vs check runs). The ForgeProvider interface itself does not change — that is the whole point of having built it.

DONE 2026-08-14. ForgeProvider.kind widened to include gitlab; GitLabProvider implements the full port with an explicit capability object asserted by toEqual so a silent drift fails. 17 contract tests, zero network, on the same stub-client harness GitHub and Gitea use. Multi-forge is now complete: GitHub, Gitea and GitLab.

EVERY SHAPE VERIFIED AGAINST A LIVE INSTANCE (gitlab.com/api/v4, project gitlab-org/cli) rather than the docs — Law 2, and it earned its keep for the third time this week. GitLab diverges further from GitHub than Gitea does: (1) project ids must be URL-ENCODED into the path (gitlab-org%2Fcli) or the request 404s in a way that reads as a permissions problem; (2) commits use `id`, not `sha`, and carry NO user object at all — only a name and email, so authorLogin is null and identity resolution falls back to the email; (3) `visibility` is a STRING (public|internal|private), not a boolean, and internal is not public; (4) merge requests use `iid` (project-scoped) as the number while `id` is global — using id would have made every PR link in the product wrong; (5) `merged` is a FIRST-CLASS state rather than closed-plus-a-flag; (6) releases have NO id, so the tag is the identity; (7) changes_count is a STRING and becomes "32+" past a display cap, which parseInt handles rather than letting NaN reach the warehouse.

CHURN IS COUNTED, NOT GUESSED — and this is where GitLab beats Gitea. GitLab returns no per-file additions/deletions either, but it DOES return the raw unified diff, so churnOfDiff counts +/- lines (excluding the +++/--- headers) for exact per-file numbers. Gitea returns neither and must record zero. So file-level hotspot ranking works on GitHub and GitLab but not on Gitea.

WEBHOOKS ARE A THIRD SCHEME. GitHub signs with HMAC-SHA256 (sha256= prefix), Gitea sends a bare hex digest, and GitLab sends X-Gitlab-Token — the SECRET ITSELF, in plaintext, with no signature over the body. The comparison is still constant-time, because a naive === leaks the secret a byte at a time to anyone who can time the endpoint. Recorded as a property in the contract test rather than left implicit: a GitLab delivery proves the sender knew the secret but says NOTHING about body integrity, which is weaker than the other two and is why TLS matters more there.

ACCEPTANCE 3 WAS UNENFORCED — the ticket referred to an "existing grep gate" that did not exist. Added packages/forge/test/capability-gate.test.ts, which fails the build if any module above the port branches on the provider NAME instead of a capability flag, and separately asserts all three adapters declare identical capability KEYS (a missing key reads as undefined, which is falsy, so a forgotten flag silently disables a feature rather than failing loudly). The gate immediately caught my own provider-factory change; rather than weaken it, exactly ONE construction site is allowlisted, because choosing which adapter to instantiate is the one decision a capability flag cannot express — there is no provider yet to ask.

ACCEPTANCE 4 REQUIRED A UI FIX NOBODY HAD NOTICED: apps/web Connections.tsx hardcoded provider:"github" in the submit body, so even with the API and all three adapters in place a customer could only ever create a GitHub connection. Added a forge picker with a credential label that changes per forge, plus the DB CHECK constraint (migration 0005) which still only permitted github|gitea and would have rejected a GitLab connection at insert time. The e2e asserts the REQUEST BODY carries the chosen provider, not merely that a dropdown renders — a picker wired to nothing would pass a visibility-only check.

NOT VERIFIED, stated plainly: no real GitLab instance has been ingested. Same gap as Gitea. The shapes are confirmed live and the contract is tested, but the GitHub smoke proved that a real-forge run catches what a self-consistent fake cannot. Needs a GitLab PAT (read_api) to close.

tickets.title: Wire the worker processors — ALL SIX queues are inert, not just backfill
acceptance: Every queue in QUEUE has a registered processor: backfill (plan + entity pages), delta (webhook deltas), enrich, reconcile, snapshot (metric compute), dlq
The worker builds a ForgeProvider per workspace from the CONNECTION credential: decrypt via the vault, wrapped in the BudgetedClient so Law 7 holds for real ingestion
Honours FORGE_BASE_URL as the API does, so a self-hosted forge or a fake is reachable from the worker too

apps/api/test/wiring.test.ts KNOWN_INERT shrinks to [] — the gate fails if a queue is left behind
notes: Filed 2026-08-13. apps/api/src/workers/index.ts constructs the runtime with processors: {} and the comment 'Empty until W2-03 supplies the real entity processors' — but W2-03 is DONE, and processBackfillJob exists and is fully tested in packages/ingest. The processors were built and never registered, so THE WORKER CONSUMES NOTHING IN PRODUCTION. A customer connects, the API enqueues a plan job, and nothing ever drains it: no error, no data, just a dashboard that stays empty.

This is the FOURTH built-but-never-mounted defect found this week (SSE events W4-18, connections/sync/webhooks W4-19, now the processors) and the most consequential. The others made a feature unreachable; this one makes the core loop inert. Same cause each time: the unit tests mount the thing themselves into a throwaway scope, so the production wiring is exercised by nothing. Worth a standing check that every route plugin and every queue processor appears in the production entrypoint, not only in a test.

Deliberately NOT attempted at the end of a long session: the wiring requires decrypting stored forge credentials inside the worker and constructing a budgeted provider per workspace. That is security-sensitive integration, not mechanical plumbing, and starting it with little context left is how credential-handling mistakes ship.

SCOPE CORRECTED 2026-08-13 after a systematic audit rather than another accidental discovery. It is not just the backfill queue: the worker registers NO processors at all, so all six declared queues are inert — delta (so accepted webhook deliveries are never applied), enrich, reconcile, snapshot (so metric snapshots are never computed) and dlq as well as backfill. Re-sized 8 -> 13. The practical consequence is that waves W2 (ingestion, 5/5 done, 25 pts) and W3 (metrics, 13/13 done, 45 pts) are code-complete and fully unit-tested but NONE of that code executes in production: today's dashboard is a view over a warehouse the SEEDER fabricates, which is exactly why it looks healthy.

PARTIAL 2026-08-13: THREE of six queues wired, the core loop among them. apps/api/src/workers/processors.ts registers backfill (both the 'plan' fan-out and the entity-page jobs), delta (webhook deltas, accepted by the receiver since W2-04 and never applied until now) and snapshot (the metric numbers every screen reads). enrich and reconcile and dlq remain inert and are still on the wiring-gate KNOWN_INERT list, which shrank 6 -> 3.

CREDENTIALS: no new crypto was written. apps/api/src/workers/forge-provider.ts resolves a repo's connection row and calls the SAME credentials.decryptCredential the API uses; a second implementation of credential handling is a second thing to get wrong. It differs from the connect-time discovery provider in two deliberate ways: it goes through the BudgetedClient because Law 7 makes the rate-limit budget law for real ingestion (discovery skips it only because a connection row may not exist yet), and the SC-12 host allowlist is derived from the configured base URL so a self-hosted forge is permitted without widening it to a wildcard. A purged connection mid-backfill returns null and the job ends quietly rather than failing into the DLQ forever.

ROUTING DETAIL: the planner orders 'checks' alongside the paginated entities, but checks are fetched per-PR through the enrich lane, not walked page-by-page at repo scope — processBackfillJob only accepts PaginatedEntity. The plan processor routes the five paginated types and reports the rest as deferredToEnrich rather than dropping them silently. VERIFIED: the worker boots with real processors and reports healthz 200. NOT YET VERIFIED: data actually flowing end to end — that needs the worker running inside the e2e stack against the fake forge, which is the remaining piece of this ticket and of W12-02. Gate: lint 0, typecheck 0, test 0 (465/465), e2e 0 (37/37).

MEASURED 2026-08-13 rather than assumed, by running the worker against the fake forge and driving the real operator flow. RESULT: the PLUMBING works and the DATA FLOW is still unproven, and the reason is the fake, not the product. Evidence: connect + repo-select created fixture-org/alpha-service; the plan job fanned out into five per-entity jobs carrying the planner's own jobIds (bf-<id>-commits/-prs/-issues/-releases/-deployments); Redis shows 18 completed and 0 failed. But the repo sits at pending_backfill with 0 commits, 0 PRs and no sync_cursors, because e2e/helpers/fake-forge.ts only implements /user/repos and /hooks — every entity fetch 404d and the jobs completed against empty results.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE REMAINING WORK: it is smaller and better understood than 'run the worker in the e2e stack'. The fake forge needs entity endpoints (commits, pulls, issues, releases, deployments) returning fixture pages, and then the assertion is simply that alpha-service gains rows and flips off pending_backfill. ALSO WORTH CHECKING while doing it: a 404 from the forge produced a COMPLETED job with no error and no cursor. That is defensible for a genuinely empty repo but indistinguishable from a broken endpoint, and a backfill that silently completes against a 404 is exactly the kind of quiet failure this project keeps finding.

NARROWED 2026-08-13 to a single reproducible symptom, with the fake no longer the blocker. The fake forge now serves entity pages (commits/pulls in GitHub's REST shapes, parsed by the real normalize.ts) and sends x-ratelimit-* headers on every response, which GitHub always does and whose absence the BudgetedClient reads (Law 7). Neither change made rows appear. THE SYMPTOM, exactly: the plan job COMPLETES and returns {planned:5, deferredToEnrich:1} — so planning, the provider, credential decryption and the fan-out all work — but the five per-entity jobs go straight to BullMQ's DELAYED set and never execute. completed=1 (the plan), failed=0, delayed=5. processPlan adds them with a jobId and NO delay option, so the delay is not coming from the call site. Next session starts there: instrument or read why an add() without delay lands in delayed. Everything upstream is proven; this is the last link.

ROOT-CAUSED AND FIXED 2026-08-13 (second session). The previous note above is WRONG and is left in place only so the mistake is not repeated: the five entity jobs did NOT sit unexecuted in the delayed set. They RAN, threw, and went to delayed awaiting exponential-backoff retry. The signature is unambiguous - attemptsMade=1 and delay=30000 exactly matching RETRY[ingest.backfill].backoff.delay; failed=0 only because attempts (5) were not exhausted. Nothing was injecting a delay at the call site, which is why none was ever found there. LESSON: read the job hashes in Redis (failedReason / stacktrace / atm) before theorising about queue state.

THE ACTUAL BLOCKER was SC-12. Every entity job died on ForgeSsrfError "scheme must be https, got http:" because the e2e fake forge is http://127.0.0.1:9099, which violates the guard three ways (http scheme, IP-literal host, not on the allowlist). Fixed with an operator-only, loopback-only escape hatch (allowInsecureLoopback, off by default, allowlist still enforced). Defensible because the forge base URL is NOT user input anywhere: it comes from the operator FORGE_BASE_URL env at the composition root and no route or UI accepts one, so an operator opting in gains nothing they did not already have. A LAN forge over plain http stays rejected - that is a separate posture decision for the founder.

tickets.title: Broaden enrichment to per-parent detail fetches; survive un-hookable repos
acceptance: Enrichment covers per-PR reviews and per-head-SHA check runs alongside per-commit churn, per the founder decision of 2026-08-13
sync_status `live` requires BOTH halves of enrichment drained, not just churn
The fake forge serves reviews and check runs, closing W12-02 acceptance 1
PR detail renders pr-reviews and pr-checks for an ingested repo, asserted in e2e
Webhook registration failure is non-fatal, so a public repo the operator does not administer still backfills
notes: FOUNDER DECISION 2026-08-13: broaden enrichment from "per-commit file churn" to "per-parent detail fetches". Reviews (per PR number) and check runs (per head SHA) are nested fetches keyed on a row the history phase already ingested — structurally identical to commit churn and unlike every paginated history entity, which is walked page-by-page at repo scope. This resolves the inconsistency where INGESTION §3 listed `checks` in the HISTORY entity order even though processBackfillJob only accepts PaginatedEntity precisely because checks cannot be walked that way. No new queue: ingest.enrich already carries the right priority and retry policy, so this adds job kinds (commitFiles, prDetail).

upsertReviews and upsertCheckRuns were both fully built, fully tested and called by NOTHING until this ticket — the sixth instance of that pattern here. The visible symptom was PR detail rendering an empty reviews section for every ingested repo.

SCHEMA: added pull_requests.enriched_at (migration 0004, one additive nullable column). A per-PR marker, NOT a repo-level high-watermark: enrich jobs run concurrently and complete out of order, so a watermark could advance past PRs that never ran and report enrichment drained — flipping the repo to `live` with reviews missing. Counting child rows cannot work either, because a PR with genuinely zero reviews AND zero checks would look permanently pending and hold the repo at `backfilling` forever.

WEBHOOK REGISTRATION IS NOW NON-FATAL, and this was a real bug rather than test convenience. The repo row is inserted BEFORE registerWebhook and enqueuePlan comes AFTER, so an unguarded throw left the repo parked in pending_backfill with no work ever queued — stuck silently and permanently. It fails legitimately in two supported cases: a PUBLIC repo the operator does not administer (hook creation needs admin, which reading does not imply — exactly the founder smoke test), and a SELF-HOSTED install with no publicly reachable URL (D1a), where deliveries could never arrive anyway. Webhooks are a freshness optimisation; backfill loads the history and the nightly reconcile sweep repairs what a missed delivery would have carried. The failure is recorded on repos.last_error ("live updates unavailable — …") rather than swallowed, so a lagging repo is explainable.

FIXTURE BUG CAUGHT BY AN EXACT COUNT: check runs were given per-PR ids restarting at 1, and check_runs upserts on (repo_id, kind, forge_run_id, run_attempt) — so PR 12's "build" silently overwrote PR 11's and only 2 of 3 rows landed. A >0 assertion would have passed. Ids are globally unique now.
Measured: fixture-org/beta-web reaches `live` with 3 reviews, 3 check runs, 4 commit_files, 3 commits and 2 PRs; both PRs carry enriched_at. Gate: lint 0, typecheck 0, 495 unit, 40 e2e, all exit 0.

tickets.title: Auth rate limit (SC-11) makes the unit gate intermittently red
acceptance: The full unit suite passes repeatedly (10 consecutive runs) with no auth-related failures
The fix does not weaken SC-11 in production — the limit stays 10/min/IP where it matters
notes: OBSERVED 2026-08-14. `pnpm test` failed 3 tests in apps/api/src/routes/repos/index.test.ts with "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'value')", then passed 497/497 on an immediate re-run with no code change. The error is at the LOGIN step, not on data: the helper reads the oauth_state cookie off the authorize response and gets undefined, which is what a 429 looks like from that call site.

CAUSE (high confidence, not yet proven): SC-11 caps the auth flow at 10 requests per minute per IP. Vitest runs test FILES in parallel and several of them perform a real OAuth round trip against the same in-process app from the same address, so a burst can exceed the cap. e2e/global-setup.ts already documents this exact hazard and works around it by logging in ONCE for the whole Playwright run — the unit suite has no equivalent.

WHY IT SURFACED NOW: nothing in the limiter changed. W12-05/W12-06 added four test files (completion, enrich-queue, graphql, processors.reconcile), which shifts scheduling and makes the burst more likely. It is latent, not new — and it is the worst kind of red, because it points at a repo route that has nothing to do with the failure.

DO NOT fix by raising the limit globally: SC-11 is a real control (T-13/T-14 brute-force). Options worth weighing: share one authenticated session across the API route tests the way globalSetup does for e2e; make the limiter keyed per test-app instance so parallel files do not share a bucket; or make the limit configurable and set it high ONLY under NODE_ENV=test, which is the least good option because it stops exercising the control.

NOT introduced by the reconcile-sweep incident and not fixed by it — those are separate. Filed rather than fixed inline so the gate reliability work is visible instead of being absorbed into an unrelated ticket.

DONE 2026-08-14. Root cause NOT definitively proven, and that is stated deliberately rather than glossed: the flake fired once in roughly four runs beforehand and has not reappeared in 11 consecutive runs since, which is strong but not conclusive. What WAS proven is that the helper hid the evidence. Five test files each carried a copy of loginAs built entirely on non-null assertions, so any unexpected auth response surfaced as "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading value)" from a repo-route test — an error naming neither auth nor a status code, which is exactly why it could not be diagnosed after the fact.

TWO CHANGES. (1) One shared helper at apps/api/src/testing/login.ts that asserts each step and reports the actual status, with a message naming the SC-11 limit as the likely cause of a 429. If this recurs it will now say so instead of pointing at the wrong subsystem. (2) The helper CACHES the session per app instance and per user. Each login costs two requests against /auth/*, which is capped at 10/minute (AUTH_FLOW_RATE_LIMIT), and the metrics and connections suites sat exactly ON that cap at five logins each — any extra request tipped them over. Caching drops most files to two auth requests total. This mirrors what e2e/global-setup.ts already does (one login per run) for the same documented reason.

SC-11 IS UNTOUCHED. The limit is still 10/min/IP in production and the rate-limit test still exercises it directly. The fix removes needless auth traffic from the suite rather than weakening the control — raising the cap under NODE_ENV=test was considered and rejected, since it would stop exercising a real security control precisely where it is cheapest to test.
VERIFIED: 11 consecutive full unit runs, 497/497 each, zero failures (acceptance asked for 10). Plus lint 0, typecheck 0, e2e 40 passed + 1 skipped.

WORSE THAN FIRST WRITTEN: .github/workflows/ci.yml provisions NO postgres and NO redis service. What is missing is ENFORCEMENT — pnpm test exits 0 either way and CI reads only the exit code. The real number: CI has been green over 433 of 586 tests.

Local runs hid this because every live-infra test file does `import 'dotenv/config'` and .env exists on a dev machine — so `env -u DATABASE_URL` changes nothing and the local suite always reports 586/586. Reproducing the CI condition needs DOTENV_CONFIG_PATH=/dev/null.

It COUNTS the gated files by scanning for the describeIfLiveInfra marker rather than hardcoding 37, so the warning cannot drift into a lie as files are added. The count agrees independently with what vitest reports skipped (37), which is a useful cross-check that the marker scan finds the right set.

RED-CHECKED THREE WAYS: (A) no infra, flag unset -> warns, exits 0. (B) no infra, REQUIRE_LIVE_INFRA=1 -> exits 1 naming both missing vars and listing all 37 files. (C) infra present, REQUIRE_LIVE_INFRA=1 -> silent, exits 0.

GATE: lint 0, typecheck 0, REQUIRE_LIVE_INFRA=1 pnpm test -> 122 files, 586 tests, ZERO skipped. All three validators exit 0. Reporting the skip count alongside the pass count is now the honest form of a gate report on this repo.

CORRECTION, 2026-08-17, found while closing W12-10: the claim in these notes and in the commit body that "CI has been green over 433 of 586 tests" is WRONG in the reader's favour. The live-infra hole is real and the fix stands, but it was never the reason CI passed over a subset — nothing in CI has ever executed at all.

notes: FILED 2026-08-19 out of W7-04 WITH MEASUREMENTS: a production build gives WidgetRegistry 175 KB gz and index 110 KB gz, so initial JS is ~285 KB gz against a 200 KB budget. The 175 KB chunk is the widget registry pulling ECharts in eagerly — every screen pays for charts even when it renders none.
size-limit and Lighthouse are NOT in docs/TECH_STACK.md; adding either is a stop-and-ask for Brad. The measurement above needed neither — build output plus gzip is enough to enforce a budget in CI.

DONE 2026-08-19. ECharts now loads with a dynamic import, so it lands in its own chunk instead of the entry bundle. Initial JS went from ~285 KB gz to 110.0 KB gz against a 200 KB budget — measured from dist/index.html, not estimated.

THE CAUSE WAS A VALUE IMPORT WHERE A TYPE IMPORT WOULD DO. Chart.tsx imported initChart as a value, which pulled echarts into the widget registry chunk, so every screen paid 175 KB gz for charts it might never render. The types are now imported with  and the runtime module inside the effect.

THE LAZY LOAD IS CANCELLABLE: a component unmounted mid-import would otherwise create a chart on a detached node and leak it. The effect sets a cancelled flag and the async create() checks it before touching the DOM.
IT MEASURES WHAT THE BROWSER FETCHES BEFORE FIRST PAINT — scripts AND modulepreload links — and deliberately excludes lazily-imported chunks. Counting those would punish the very fix being made.

THREE UNIT TESTS NEEDED AWAITING, NOT CHANGING: they asserted initChart was called synchronously, which stopped being true when the import became dynamic. The behaviour is unchanged; the timing moved by a microtask. e2e confirmed charts still render in a real browser before the unit tests were touched, so the failure was correctly read as a timing assertion rather than a broken chart.

NOT DONE, SAID PLAINLY: the LCP and API p95 gates. k6 is in TECH_STACK but is a system binary and is not installed here; no LCP measurement was taken. Those two acceptance criteria are unmet and are NOT claimed. The bundle budget — the one that was actually breached — is now enforced.
